title: Static and Dynamic Routing
tagline: How a packet chooses its next hop, and who tells it.
summary: Routing is one decision — longest prefix match — repeated at every hop. This module covers routing tables, static and default routes, metrics and administrative distance, then introduces RIP, OSPF and BGP and what each is actually for.
objectives: Explain Layer 2 forwarding versus Layer 3 routing in terms of what changes at each hop.
Read a routing table and identify connected, local, static and dynamic routes.
Apply longest prefix match to real entries and explain why the most specific wins.
Explain metrics and administrative distance, and why implementations differ.
Describe distance-vector, link-state and path-vector routing and where each fits.
Recognise routing loops and the symptoms they produce.
key_questions: How does a router choose between two routes to the same destination?
What is longest prefix match, with an example where it surprises people?
What is the difference between static and dynamic routing?
Why does OSPF use link state while RIP uses hop count?
What is an autonomous system, and why does BGP exist?

assessment.prompt: A routing table has 10.0.0.0/8 via A, 10.1.0.0/16 via B, and 10.1.2.0/24 via C. Where does a packet to 10.1.2.55 go?
options: It is sent to all three
assessment.explanation: Longest prefix match: /24 is more specific than /16 and /8, so C wins regardless of metric.

why_wrong.1: Only correct if no more specific route existed.

assessment.prompt: What does an administrative distance (or preference) do?
options: Selects between routes to the same prefix learned from different sources
Breaks ties between routes with different prefix lengths
Sets the TTL of outgoing packets
assessment.explanation: When two sources advertise the same prefix, the source with the lower distance wins; metric then breaks ties within one protocol.

why_wrong.2: Prefix length decides first; distance only compares identical prefixes.

assessment.prompt: Explain longest prefix match and why 'the most specific route wins even if it is a worse path' is a design decision, not a bug.

checklist.text: A router compares the destination against every prefix and selects the one with the longest match.
Prefix length is checked before metric or administrative distance.
Specificity encodes intent: a /24 usually represents a deliberately configured policy for that subnet.
Deaggregation and more-specific routes can therefore override a provider's routing, accidentally or on purpose.
Verification with ip route get shows the chosen entry.

assessment.reference: Longest prefix match is evaluated before any metric comparison: the router finds all entries that contain the destination and picks the one with the longest mask. That is a policy statement — the more precisely an operator describes a network, the more authority that statement has. It is why a leaked /24 can override an aggregate /8, why traffic engineering uses more-specifics, and why a missing more-specific route sends traffic to a default gateway that cannot handle it. ip route get shows the winning entry directly.
